title: The Balcons, A Chamonix Running Week Facing Mont Blanc

bestPeriod.note: Lac Blanc and the Aiguillette des Posettes hold hard snow into early July; most refuges shut between mid and late September.

summary: Seven days on the two great balcony trails of the Chamonix valley, with the lifts doing the climbing and the recovery days built into the plan.
hook: Chamonix runs on two horizontal lines. The Grand Balcon Nord traverses the Aiguilles Rouges side of nothing, it clings to the Mont Blanc massif itself, under the granite spires, on moraine and slab. The Grand Balcon Sud sits opposite on the Aiguilles Rouges, in the sun, looking straight across at the whole range. Between them and the lifts that reach them, you can build a week of genuine alpine running without ever carrying a rope or sleeping above 2,000 m.

snapshot.Base(s): Chamonix-Mont-Blanc (all week; Argentière is the quieter alternative)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: approx. 105-125 km, 6,500-7,500 m vert; moraine, granite slab, alpine singletrack, forest balcon
snapshot.Getting There: Geneva (GVA) → shared shuttle or coach to Chamonix, approx. 1h15; or rail via Saint-Gervais and the Mont-Blanc Express
snapshot.Who It Suits: Experienced mountain runners comfortable with exposure, ladders and 1,500 m descents

itinerary.title: Petit Balcon Sud and the Chalet de la Floria
itinerary.morning: Arrive, get your Carte d'Hôte from the accommodation, it covers the valley buses and the Mont-Blanc Express train between Servoz and Vallorcine, and you will use it every day.
itinerary.afternoon: Open the legs low. The Petit Balcon Sud is a forest traverse at around 1,200 m running the whole length of the valley. Pick it up above Chamonix, run north-east to the Chalet de la Floria, a flower-covered buvette with the best cheap terrace view in the valley, then descend to Les Praz and jog the Arve riverside path home.
itinerary.evening: Eat early. Altitude in Chamonix is only 1,035 m, but you will feel the first days regardless.
itinerary.dayStats: 13 km, 500 m vert. Grade T1-T2, forest singletrack and root, no exposure. Water: Chamonix town fountains, Chalet de la Floria, Les Praz. Bail-out: the balcon is 20-30 min above the valley floor at any point.

itinerary.title: Grand Balcon Nord: Plan de l'Aiguille to Montenvers
itinerary.morning: First cable car on the Aiguille du Midi, but only to the mid-station at Plan de l'Aiguille (2,317 m). From the Refuge du Plan de l'Aiguille the Grand Balcon Nord traverses east under the Aiguille du Midi, the Blaitière and the Grands Charmoz on moraine, slab and scree, with the Mer de Glace opening below.
itinerary.afternoon: Reach Montenvers (1,913 m) and its hotel and railway station. Refill, then descend either by the rack railway or on foot down the Grand Balcon Nord's lower path and the Signal Forbes trail to Chamonix. Choose the train if the quads are new to this.
itinerary.dayStats: 14-18 km, 400 m vert (lift-assisted), 700-1,300 m descent. Grade T3 in sections, cable-secured slabs, moraine crossings, real exposure above the glacier. Water: Refuge du Plan de l'Aiguille, Montenvers. Bail-out: the Montenvers rack railway; the Aiguille du Midi cable car back down from Plan de l'Aiguille.

itinerary.title: Recovery: Les Bois, the Arve and Vallorcine
itinerary.morning: Genuinely easy. Run the flat Arve path from Chamonix through Les Praz to Les Bois and the hamlet of Le Lavancher, on gravel and packed earth, then loop back. Forty-five to sixty minutes, nose-breathing.
itinerary.afternoon: Take the Mont-Blanc Express to Vallorcine (free with the Carte d'Hôte) and walk, do not run, the valley floor to the Cascade de Bérard. Coffee, then train home.
itinerary.evening: Look hard at the forecast. Days 4 and 6 both need clear mornings.
itinerary.dayStats: 10 km run, 150 m vert. Grade T1, riverside gravel. Water: fountains in Chamonix, Les Praz, Argentière and Vallorcine, all drinkable. Bail-out: trivial, the train parallels the whole route.

itinerary.title: Aiguillette des Posettes and the Col de Balme
itinerary.morning: The quality day. Train to Le Tour and climb the ridge of the Aiguillette des Posettes (2,201 m) as one sustained effort, roughly 850 m of gain on a clean, runnable spur with the whole Mont Blanc range at your back. This ridge appears in the closing stages of the big Chamonix ultra courses and it is worth understanding why: it is steep enough to hurt and smooth enough to keep running.
itinerary.afternoon: From the summit, drop north-west to the Col des Montets and Tré-le-Champ, or extend north-east over the Col de Balme (2,191 m) on the Swiss frontier and descend to Charamillon for the gondola down to Le Tour. Train back.
itinerary.evening: Refuel properly. Savoyard food is heavy and appropriate.
itinerary.dayStats: 18-22 km, 1,050 m vert, 1,050-1,300 m descent. Grade T2, with a T3 rocky section on the Posettes crest and moderate ridge exposure. Water: Le Tour village fountain, the Charamillon mid-station buvette, Tré-le-Champ. Bail-out: the Charamillon/Balme gondola from Le Tour; the Col des Montets road with valley buses.

itinerary.title: Rest day
itinerary.morning: No running at all. Chamonix rewards a slow morning, the Maison de la Montagne, the guides' office noticeboard with the day's conditions, the market on Place du Mont-Blanc on Saturdays.
itinerary.afternoon: If you must move, ride the Montenvers train and walk the gallery to look at the Mer de Glace, which is retreating fast enough that the staircase down to it is extended most years. Otherwise: the Chamonix outdoor pool at the Centre Sportif, and a long nap.
itinerary.evening: Pack for Day 6 tonight. It starts early.
itinerary.dayStats: Rest. 0 km. Water: everywhere. Bail-out: not applicable.

itinerary.title: Grand Balcon Sud: Bellachat, Brévent, Flégère, Lac Blanc
itinerary.morning: The week's big day, and it starts on foot. Bus to Les Houches and climb the Bellachat trail, a long, steady 1,400 m through forest then open alpage past the Refuge de Bellachat to Le Brévent (2,525 m). Sunrise on the way up puts Mont Blanc directly in front of you the whole climb.
itinerary.afternoon: From Brévent, run the Grand Balcon Sud north-east across Planpraz and the Aiguillette des Houches side of the ridge to La Flégère (1,877 m), then climb to Lac Blanc (2,352 m) and its refuge. Return along the balcon and descend to Argentière, or take the Flégère cable car down to Les Praz if the day has taken enough. Bus or train home.
itinerary.dayStats: 28-32 km, 2,100 m vert, 1,700-2,200 m descent. Grade T2-T3; the Lac Blanc approach and the Tête aux Vents area include bolted metal ladders and cable on granite slabs, with genuine exposure. Water: Refuge de Bellachat, Brévent and Planpraz stations, La Flégère restaurant, Refuge du Lac Blanc. Bail-out: three separate lifts intersect this route, Brévent/Planpraz, Flégère, and the valley buses at either end.

itinerary.title: Loriaz or the Bois du Bouchet, then out
itinerary.morning: Short and beautiful. Train to Vallorcine and run the climb to the Refuge de Loriaz (2,020 m), a quiet alpage terrace looking straight down the valley at the Aiguille Verte, then descend the same way. If the legs are finished, jog the flat Bois du Bouchet loops in Chamonix instead.
itinerary.afternoon: Shower, one last fondue or one last salad, and the shuttle to Geneva.
itinerary.dayStats: 12 km, 700 m vert. Grade T2, alpage path and forest. Water: Vallorcine fountain, Refuge de Loriaz (staffed in season). Bail-out: single valley path back to Vallorcine station.

accommodationStrategy.name: Auberge de Jeunesse de Chamonix
accommodationStrategy.description: Sits on the valley bus line at the Les Houches end, which is exactly where Day 6 begins, and has drying space, self-catering, a bag store and a genuinely international climbing and running crowd. The cheapest way to spend a week in one of the most expensive valleys in the Alps.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotels and apartments around Argentière
accommodationStrategy.description: Argentière is quieter than Chamonix, 200 m higher, and closer to the Posettes, Balme and Lac Blanc trailheads, three of this week's six sessions start nearer here. It has a train station on the Mont-Blanc Express, a supermarket and enough restaurants. Choose it if you value sleep over nightlife.
accommodationStrategy.booking: 3-4 months ahead, and avoid the UTMB week entirely unless you are running it.

accommodationStrategy.name: Self-catering apartments in Chamonix Sud
accommodationStrategy.description: An apartment with a washing machine and a kitchen changes a running week. Chamonix Sud is walking distance to the Aiguille du Midi and Brévent lift stations and to the bus hub, which removes a transfer from every morning. Look for a ground-floor unit with a ski locker, it becomes the wet kit room.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €150, €260 per night for two to four

logistics.emergency: 112. Mountain rescue in the Chamonix valley is run by the PGHM; calling 112 routes you to them. Give your position as a named trail plus altitude, not GPS coordinates read aloud.
logistics.weather: Afternoon convective build-up is routine from mid-July. Météo-France publishes a specific Mont-Blanc massif bulletin; the guides' office in Chamonix posts it daily. Be off the Balcon Sud ladders before storms arrive.
logistics.bookingWindows: Chamonix accommodation for August should be booked in spring. The UTMB week in late August fills the entire valley and doubles prices, either plan around it or embrace it.
logistics.money: The Chamonix Mont-Blanc Multipass covers the valley's lifts and the Montenvers train; a single day runs to roughly €70, €90 per adult, with 2-6 day passes bringing the daily rate down substantially. Buy the number of days you will actually use, not more.

other.label: The Carte d'Hôte is free and essential
other.text: Every registered accommodation issues one at check-in. It covers the valley bus network and the Mont-Blanc Express train between Servoz and Vallorcine. It does not cover the lifts.

other.label: Glacial water is not drinkable and no filter helps
other.text: The Arve and every torrent draining a glacier carries suspended rock flour. Use the village fountains, Chamonix, Les Praz, Argentière, Le Tour, Vallorcine all have them, and the refuges.

other.label: Refuge water in late summer
other.text: High refuges like Lac Blanc rely on stored or piped supply and can be short in a dry August; some charge for water or ask you to buy a drink. Never plan a day whose only water is a single high refuge.

other.label: Money
other.text: Cards everywhere, including refuges, though signal can fail. Carry €30, €40.

other.label: Drones
other.text: Prohibited over much of the massif and inside the Réserve Naturelle des Aiguilles Rouges, which covers the whole Balcon Sud. Assume no.

other.label: The Aiguilles Rouges reserve
other.text: Dogs banned, camping banned, staying on marked paths required, no picking anything. Rangers patrol Lac Blanc.

proTips: Take the first Aiguille du Midi cabin at around 07:00 and get off at Plan de l'Aiguille. The Grand Balcon Nord is a narrow traverse; an hour earlier means an empty path and firmer overnight-frozen moraine.

Run the Grand Balcon Sud south-west to north-east in the afternoon and the Grand Balcon Nord in the morning. The Aiguilles Rouges side catches evening light on Mont Blanc; the Mont Blanc side is in shadow and cold by 16:00.
Buy lift passes as a multi-day Multipass only if you will use three or more days. Otherwise the free valley train plus one single lift ticket beats it easily.
Climb Bellachat from Les Houches on foot rather than riding Brévent up. It is the finest sustained climb in the valley, it faces Mont Blanc the whole way, and it is almost empty before 09:00.
The Chalet de la Floria and the Refuge de Bellachat are both cheap places to refill and both are staffed daily in season, worth more to your planning than any high refuge.
Check the guides' office conditions board in Chamonix each evening. It reports snow on the Lac Blanc and Posettes approaches, which is the specific information that decides your next day.
If the Balcon Sud is stormed off, the Petit Balcon Nord runs the shaded valley side at 1,200 m from Argentière to Les Tines and stays runnable in almost any weather.

packingNotes: Shoes with sticky rubber and a rock plate. The Balcon Nord is polished granite slab and moraine block; lugs matter less than grip on rock.
A light pack that carries 1.5 L, a shell and a spare layer without bouncing. Half of these days are three to six hours from a road.
Wind shell plus a waterproof, different garments, both needed on Day 6.
Gloves. The ladders near Tête aux Vents are cold metal and often wet.
Sunglasses with real UV rating and high-factor sunscreen: you are at 2,300 m on reflective granite and snow patches.
Poles for the Bellachat climb and the Montenvers descent.
A headtorch for the pre-dawn start on Day 6.
A buff or light beanie, the Balcon Nord holds cold air off the Mer de Glace all morning.
Cash of €30, €40 for refuges with intermittent card signal.
A dry bag for the phone: afternoon storms here arrive faster than you can descend.
whatCouldGoWrong: **Storm on the Grand Balcon Sud.** The ladders and slabs above Tête aux Vents are the last place to be in lightning. Fallback: descend immediately to La Flégère and take the cable car down; it is 25-40 minutes from most of the balcon.

**The Aiguille du Midi is closed for wind and Day 2 has no start.** Fallback: run the Grand Balcon Nord in reverse from Montenvers, reached by the rack railway which operates in weather that grounds the cable car.

**Old snow on the Lac Blanc approach in early July.** North-facing slabs hold hard névé and people fall on them every season. Fallback: check the guides' office board, and substitute the Aiguillette des Posettes, which clears earlier.

**Quads destroyed by Day 5.** Two 1,500 m descents in a week is a lot of eccentric load. Fallback: take the lifts down. The Day 5 rest day is structural, not filler, skipping it is how this week ends in a strained calf.

**Everything is full and twice the price.** If your dates land on the UTMB week in late August, the valley is at capacity. Fallback: base in Vallorcine or Les Houches, both on the free valley transport, or move the trip to the first half of September when the refuges are still open and the crowds have gone.
